title: How Coelacanths Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the coelacanth, a deep-sea lobe-finned fish thought extinct for about 66-80 million years until a specimen was caught off South Africa in 1938 and identified by Marjorie Courtney-Latimer and J.L.B. Smith. They cover Mark Erdmann's discovery of a living coelacanth in Indonesia decades later, the two surviving species, their unusual anatomy (oil-filled notochord, hinged skull, rostral electrosensory organ, vestigial lungs, fatty skull), live-bearing reproduction, their evolutionary significance as a supposed "missing link," conservation status, and other "living fossil" fish such as bowfin, gar, hagfish and sturgeon. The episode ends with a listener mail about Bob Dorough of Schoolhouse Rock and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck banter about revisiting an old video on coelacanths and note that the coelacanth is interesting despite a thin HowStuffWorks article, relying on Smithsonian and Mental Floss sources.

segments.title: Discovery of the coelacanth in 1938 South Africa
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Devonian origins of the coelacanth, its supposed extinction about 80 million years ago, and the 1938 catch by trawler Captain Hendrik Goosen off South Africa. Marjorie Courtney-Latimer examined the fish at the East London Museum, had it taken to a taxidermist, and sent scales and a sketch to J.L.B. Smith, who identified it and named the species after her.

segments.title: Erdmann's Indonesian coelacanth and the two living species
segments.summary: About sixty years later, biologist Mark Erdmann saw a coelacanth in an Indonesian market, offered a bounty, and received a live-caught specimen, a brown fish later described as a new species. The hosts discuss the two living species, their geographic ranges (Comoros area and Indonesia), and the extinct relatives, including the toothless Megalocoelacanthus.

segments.title: Living fossil label and slow evolution
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why coelacanths are called living fossils, citing a genome study suggesting slower evolutionary rates, and debate whether they have really changed. They also discuss why the fossil record gap may reflect poor fossilization conditions near volcanic rock.

segments.title: Habitat, behavior and hunting
segments.summary: The hosts describe coelacanth habitat in deep water and caves at roughly 500 to 800 feet in the twilight zone, nocturnal hunting, passive ambush feeding, and a Tasmanian population not in caves that is listed as endangered. They discuss the rostral organ that may detect electrical signals from prey and the habit of hovering nose-down.

segments.title: Anatomy: hinged skull, notochord and vestigial lungs
segments.summary: The hosts cover the coelacanth's hinged cranium that lets it open its mouth wide, the name meaning hollow spine from its oil-filled notochord, the fatty skull with a small brain, and vestigial lungs that develop in embryos but serve no purpose in adults.

segments.title: Reproduction, live birth and missing link status
segments.summary: The hosts discuss unknown male reproductive anatomy, ovoviviparity with about three years of gestation, cannibalistic mothers, a study of two pregnant females suggesting a single father, and the Mental Floss note about the operetta by hematologist Charles Rand. They then discuss the coelacanth's limb-like fins and its former status as a missing link to tetrapods, which the genome later complicated.

segments.title: Edibility, endangered status and other living fossil fish
segments.summary: The hosts note coelacanths are not eaten and are unpleasant and possibly toxic, cover their endangered status and small population estimates, then survey other living fossil fish: bowfin, gar, hagfish and sturgeon, with a brief tangent about a shark jumping into a boat.

segments.title: Listener mail about Bob Dorough and Schoolhouse Rock
segments.summary: A listener named Pete writes that his stepfather Bob Dorough, a Schoolhouse Rock creator, heard the hosts praise him on a prior episode and that the hosts' praise warmed the family's hearts.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and list social media and email contacts and the website for more information.
